doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
title: Guitar in big-band rhythm sections
summary: They discuss why bandleaders dropped guitar, how chugging guitarists tied down rhythm sections, and the good players like Freddie Green and Barry Galbraith.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: That's when they had the electric guitar players who were more like the bebop guitar players.
But they were comping, they weren’t, you know playing…
Yeah, like Sal Salvador and Ralph Blaze.
Yeah, who weren’t Freddie Green style guitar players, they were…
Well that was really out, the only one doing it was Freddie.
And a couple guys around in New York who when they got work, like Barry Galbraith and…
Steve Jordan was great he was with Boyd when I first joined, but then Boyd dropped the guitar.
For the same reason I assume.

Same thing, everybody wanted to go with three piece rhythm sections; sort of like Dizzy’s band and Billy Eckstine. Well, in those days most guitar players used to not be a good thing to have. I mean they didn’t play like Freddie Green, they chugged away, like chug, chug, chug, chug and that did tie down a rhythm section, I’d’ve wanted to get rid of it too, even Billy Bauer did that.
Well a lot of the, like best rhythm guitar players were, either they played without amps or they turned it up just enough so that you…
It was just amplified a tad, but very little, you heard like, “chick-chick-chick” rather than…
Barry did that, Herb Ellis was wonderful. Yeah, these were the good guitar players, Chuck Wayne was good.
Um-hm, but in any case that was…
But Artie’s band, we had Jimmy Raney in that band so it was, yeah, it was just an all- around good band.
